Check that `lsmod | grep nvidia` shows the nvidia modules, `cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version` returns the driver version, and `find /usr/ -iname libnvidia-ml.so` finds the library. If those are fine, you may have forgotten to reboot the node after installing the driver packages.

instruction: Ollama on our SUSE AI cluster is running but only using the CPU.
output:
Make sure the pod can actually get a GPU:
1. Enable GPU passthrough in the Ollama Helm chart values. Without it the container runs but uses only the CPU.
2. Request the GPU resource with `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` of `nvidia.com/gpu: 1`.
3. Optionally set a nodeSelector such as `accelerator: nvidia-gpu`.
When the GPU is detected, Ollama logs 'looking for compatible GPUs' followed by an 'inference compute' line with `library=cuda`.

instruction: OpenSearch pods from the SUSE AI Library won't start properly. Anything host-level I'm missing?
output: OpenSearch needs `vm.max_map_count` set to at least 262144, for both single-node and multi-node setups. Check the current value with `cat /proc/sys/vm/max_map_count`. To raise it, add `vm.max_map_count=262144` to `/etc/sysctl.conf` and run `sudo sysctl -p`.

instruction: Open WebUI install from the SUSE AI library complains about cert-manager. It used to just work.
output: Earlier releases installed cert-manager automatically with Open WebUI. Now cert-manager is no longer part of the Open WebUI Helm chart and has to be installed separately first. Install it from Application Collection with `helm upgrade --install cert-manager oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/cert-manager -n <CERT_MANAGER_NAMESPACE> --set crds.enabled=true --set 'global.imagePullSecrets[0].name'=application-collection`. Then rerun the Open WebUI installation.

instruction: Our new SLES 16 server shows up in SUSE Customer Center with the hostname 'agama'. How do I fix it?
output: If no hostname is set during installation, the system registers with the installer's transient hostname `agama`. SCC is not updated automatically when the hostname changes later. To fix it, set the correct hostname on the system, deregister it with SUSEConnect, and register it again. Next time, set the hostname in Agama before registering.

instruction: An old SysV init script from a vendor doesn't run on SLES 16. Workaround?
output: SUSE Linux 16 removes SysV init script support, and all services must use standard systemd units. Rewrite the vendor's init script as a systemd service unit, or ask the vendor for one. Unlike SLE 15, there is no SysV compatibility layer to fall back on.

instruction: After upgrading to SLES 16 some config files seem to have reverted. Where do I look?
output: Look for `*.rpmnew` and `*.rpmsave` files in `/etc`. A `.rpmnew` file contains the new default configuration and leaves your modified file in place. A `.rpmsave` file is a copy of your modified configuration that was replaced by the new default. Find them with `find /etc/ -name "*.rpmnew" -o -name "*.rpmsave"` and merge the changes you want.

instruction: RKE2 restarted on its own right after I applied the GPU Operator manifest. Should I worry?
output: This is expected. The NVIDIA operator restarts containerd with a hangup call, which restarts RKE2. After about a minute, check that the GPU shows up as an allocatable resource with `kubectl get node $NODENAME -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable}'`. Also check that the containerd config includes the NVIDIA runtime: `grep nvidia /var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml`.

instruction: Compare bci-base, bci-minimal and bci-micro.
output:
All three share the SLES base, glibc, CA certificates and the RPM database, but differ in tooling and size:
1. BCI-Base (about 135 MB) has bash, rpm and Zypper with the SLE_BCI repository. It is the most flexible for building images.
2. BCI-Minimal (about 48 MB) drops Zypper but keeps the rpm binary, so it can install RPMs without dependency resolution.
3. BCI-Micro (about 28 MB) also drops rpm and is meant for static or self-contained binaries from multi-stage builds.
Sizes are for the 15.7 tags.

instruction: What's the difference between `zypper patch` and `zypper update` on SLES?
output: `zypper patch` installs officially released patches that apply to your system. If it succeeds, no vulnerable package version remains installed unless you confirm an exception, and it reports a conflict if a package is considered vulnerable. `zypper update` installs newer versions of installed packages even from repositories that provide no patches. It skips problematic packages, such as locked ones. SUSE describes patching as the most reliable way to update SLES.

instruction: How does updating differ between SLES 16 and SUSE Linux Micro?
output: SLES 16 is a traditional, non-transactional OS: you update it in place with Zypper, for example with `zypper patch`. Transactional updates are not supported on SUSE Linux 16. SUSE Linux Micro has a read-only root file system and is changed only through `transactional-update`. The changes go into a new Btrfs snapshot that becomes active on reboot and can be rolled back.

instruction: What are the biggest changes between SLE 15 and SLES 16 that an admin should know about?
output:
Main changes in SUSE Linux 16 compared with SLE 15:
1. YaST is gone. Agama is the installer, Cockpit handles 1:1 management, and Ansible or SUSE Multi-Linux Manager handle automation.
2. Service Packs are replaced by annual minor releases (16.0, 16.1, ...).
3. SELinux in enforcing mode replaces AppArmor.
4. NetworkManager replaces wicked, and SysV init scripts are removed.
5. Wayland replaces X11, and Xen host and PV guest support is removed.

instruction: How does the SLES 16 release and support cycle work compared with SLES 15 service packs?
output: SLE 15 used Service Packs, each with 18 months of general support and a 6-month overlap. SUSE Linux 16 uses minor releases (16.0, 16.1, and so on), released every November. Each has 24 months of general support with a 12-month overlap with the next release. The final minor release, 16.6, gets 48 months of general support, which completes a 10-year lifecycle expected to end in November 2035. LTS options extend support further.

instruction: SUSE Linux Micro images come in 'base' and 'default' flavors. What's the difference?
output: Both subtypes contain the core OS plus Podman. The default subtype also includes the virtualization stack, Cockpit and salt-minion. Every image type is offered in one of these two subtypes: raw disk, self-install, PXE, virtual machine and cloud images.

instruction: Application Collection: user account with access token vs service account — when do I use which?
output: With a user account and access token, you authenticate on your own behalf. You inherit the subscriptions of every organization you belong to, and you can create as many tokens as you like. A service account belongs to one organization and only has that organization's subscriptions. Only organization admins can create one, it is meant for machine-to-machine use, and it generally has less restrictive pull rate limits. Service accounts cannot sign in to the web application.

instruction: How are subscriptions structured in SUSE Application Collection?
output: Each application is labelled with the minimum subscription needed to pull it, and every pull requires authentication. The subscriptions are Free, Prime (with SUSE Rancher Prime), Extended and SUSE AI. A subscription includes its own content plus the content of the subscriptions it supersedes. For example, SUSE AI includes Free and Prime content. Paid subscriptions are assigned to organizations, not to individual users.

instruction: In SUSE AI, what's the difference between charts from SUSE Application Collection and charts from SUSE Registry?
output: SUSE builds Application Collection artifacts itself, and they are pulled from `dp.apps.rancher.io` with an Application Collection username and access token. The AI applications on SUSE Registry (`registry.suse.com`) are not built by the SUSE build system. They are mirrored upstream projects with attached supply-chain artifacts, and you access them with the username `regcode` and your SUSE AI SCC registration code. SUSE AI uses both. For example, Ollama and Open WebUI come from `oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/`, while Qdrant and LiteLLM come from `oci://registry.suse.com/ai/charts/`.

instruction: How do the pieces of a SUSE AI deployment fit together?
output:
A SUSE AI deployment is built up in this order:
1. A supported OS (SLES or SUSE Linux Micro) on each node, with NVIDIA drivers on the GPU nodes.
2. SUSE Rancher Prime: RKE2 as the Kubernetes distribution.
3. SUSE Rancher Prime installed on a Kubernetes cluster, with the downstream AI cluster registered to it.
4. The NVIDIA GPU Operator on the RKE2 cluster, with GPU nodes assigned to AI workloads.
5. Optionally SUSE Security, then SUSE Observability for monitoring.
6. AI Library applications installed via Helm from SUSE Application Collection and SUSE Registry.

instruction: Are SUSE BCIs supported when running on non-SUSE Kubernetes like OpenShift or EKS?
output: Yes, the container guide lists third-party container hosts as supported, including RKE, RKE2, K3s, Red Hat OpenShift, AKS, EKS and IBM Hyper Protect Platform. Support on GKE is workload-specific. SUSE supports the components of the SUSE base containers and packages from SUSE repositories, while host environment issues go to the host vendor. The container architecture must match the host architecture.

instruction: Do the language-stack BCIs follow the SLES lifecycle like bci-base does?
output: Not necessarily. General-purpose BCIs follow the lifecycle of the SLES service pack they are based on. Development Stack BCIs are supported as long as their language stack is supported, so new version tags can appear during a service pack's lifetime and older ones can go out of support. A BCI stops receiving updates once its support ends, and you are not notified. Check https://suse.com/lifecycle and the `com.suse.supportlevel` label of the tag you use.

instruction: For SUSE Observability with SUSE AI, single cluster or multi cluster?
output: You can do either. A single cluster for both SUSE AI and SUSE Observability is simpler and can use internal cluster DNS, and the guide positions it for testing and proofs of concept. Separate dedicated clusters isolate workloads and are recommended for production. With separate clusters, you must expose SUSE Observability's collector endpoint and API to the AI cluster, for example via an Ingress with TLS. Either way you need access to SUSE Application Collection, a SUSE AI subscription and a SUSE Observability license.

instruction: How does Kubernetes decide to put a SUSE AI workload on a GPU node: resource requests or node labels?
output: The two methods can be combined. With a resource request, you ask for `nvidia.com/gpu` (for example `limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1`), which the NVIDIA GPU Operator exposes, and the scheduler places the pod on a node with free GPUs. With labels and node selectors, you label GPU nodes (for example `accelerator=nvidia-gpu`) and set a matching `nodeSelector` in the chart values. The selector is optional but useful to restrict workloads to specific GPU nodes.

instruction: transactional-update apply vs. a normal reboot after transactional-update: what are the trade-offs?
output: With a normal transactional update, the new snapshot becomes active on reboot. The switch is atomic and easy to roll back. `transactional-update apply` mounts the new `/etc`, `/usr` and `/boot` into the running system so you skip the reboot, but it is not atomic. Processes may briefly see an inconsistent system, services are not restarted automatically, and normal boot-time initialization is bypassed. Use `apply` only for simple package installs or removals, never for full system updates.

instruction: What are the ways to install SUSE AI Library applications?
output:
There are three methods:
1. Install each application with the Helm CLI, in dependency order: cert-manager first, then a vector database, then Ollama, Open WebUI and the rest.
2. Use SUSE AI Deployer, a meta Helm chart that installs the components you need together.
3. Use SUSE AI Lifecycle Manager, a Rancher UI extension that installs applications from ClusterRepo repositories pointing at SUSE Application Collection and SUSE Registry.

instruction: What components does the SUSE AI vLLM chart deploy?
output:
The vLLM Helm chart in the AI Library deploys the vLLM production stack:
1. A Serving Engine that runs model inference.
2. A Router that handles OpenAI-compatible API requests.
3. Optionally, LMCache to improve caching efficiency.
4. Optionally, CacheServer as a distributed KV cache back end.
It requires NVIDIA GPUs in the cluster.

instruction: Can I still use wicked for networking on SLES 16?
output: No. SUSE Linux 16 removes wicked, and NetworkManager is the only supported network management tool. Related removals include NIS (use LDAP instead), the ISC DHCP server (use Kea) and nscd. Plan to convert wicked-based configurations to NetworkManager before migrating.

instruction: In SUSE Application Collection, what's the difference between an application, a component and an artifact?
output: An application is something you can install on its own, such as etcd or Argo CD. It is delivered either as a Helm chart, which can depend on other applications or components, or as a single container. A component is part of an application and cannot be installed stand-alone. An example is the Apache APISIX Dashboard for Apache APISIX. An artifact is the distributable package of a component's binaries, either a container image or a Helm chart, and it is updated through revisions.

instruction: Walk me through registering SLES 15 SP7 with YaST after installation.
output:
1. Start YaST › Software › Product Registration.
2. Enter the e-mail address of the SUSE account that manages your subscriptions and the registration code for SUSE Linux Enterprise Server.
3. Keep the default (SUSE Customer Center), or choose or enter a local RMT server.
4. Choose Next. In the Extension and Module Selection dialog, select at least the Basesystem and Server Applications modules plus any others you need. Extensions need their own registration codes.
5. Accept any licenses, let the package installer add the release packages, and finish with Accept.

instruction: What are the steps to register SUSE Linux Micro after deployment?
output:
1. As root, run `transactional-update register -r REGISTRATION_CODE -e EMAIL_ADDRESS`. Add `--url "https://suse_register.example.com/"` with your server's URL if you use a local registration server.
2. Reboot so the system switches to the latest snapshot.
3. The system is now registered. Check it with `SUSEConnect -s`, or see `SUSEConnect --help` for other options.

instruction: How do I roll back SUSE Linux Micro from a running system to an earlier snapshot?
output:
1. List snapshots and note the number you want: `sudo snapper list`.
2. Set it as the default: `sudo transactional-update rollback snapshot_number`. If you omit the number, the current snapshot becomes the default. `rollback last` selects the last working snapshot.
3. Reboot to boot into the new default snapshot.

instruction: How do I upgrade SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 to 6.2?
output:
1. Make sure the system is registered (`sudo transactional-update register -r REGCODE`) and fully patched (`sudo transactional-update patch`). Upgrades are supported only from the latest patch level.
2. Back up configuration and data, check free disk space on Btrfs, and shut down any KVM guests.
3. Run `sudo transactional-update migration`. This creates a new snapshot and refreshes the repositories.
4. Enter the number of the migration target and confirm the package changes with y.
5. Reboot with `sudo reboot`. If something fails, roll back to the previous snapshot.
Upgrades to 6.2 are supported from SLE Micro 5.5, 6.0 or SUSE Linux Micro 6.1.

instruction: How do I create an access token for SUSE Application Collection?
output:
1. Open the Application Collection web application (apps.rancher.io) and sign in with your SUSE Customer Center credentials.
2. Click your profile picture in the upper-right corner, then Settings.
3. Go to the Access tokens section, enter a meaningful description and click Create.
4. Copy the token from the green box. Use it with your username for docker, podman, helm, kubectl or the REST API. The page also shows ready-to-copy helper commands.

instruction: Steps to deploy an application from SUSE Application Collection onto a Kubernetes cluster with Helm?
output:
1. Make sure you have kubectl and helm access to the cluster, and an Application Collection access token or service account.
2. Log helm in: `helm registry login dp.apps.rancher.io -u <your-username-or-sa-username> -p <access-token-or-sa-secret>`.
3. Create the pull secret in the target namespace: `kubectl create secret docker-registry application-collection --docker-server=dp.apps.rancher.io --docker-username=... --docker-password=...`.
4. Review the options with `helm show values oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/<app>`.
5. Install, for example `helm install redis oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/redis --set global.imagePullSecrets={application-collection}`.

instruction: Outline the procedure to get access and install SUSE AI Library applications.
output:
1. Get the SUSE AI entitlement and confirm it at https://apps.rancher.io/. Then sign in and create an Application Collection access token.
2. Create a namespace: `kubectl create namespace <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE>`.
3. Create the `application-collection` pull secret for `dp.apps.rancher.io` and the `suse-ai-registry` secret for `registry.suse.com`, which uses the username `regcode` and your SCC registration code.
4. Run `helm registry login` for both `dp.apps.rancher.io/charts` and `registry.suse.com`.
5. Install cert-manager, then a vector database (OpenSearch or Milvus), then Ollama, Open WebUI and any other components, such as vLLM, mcpo, PyTorch, Qdrant, LiteLLM, MLflow and Kubeflow.

instruction: How do I install the NVIDIA open GPU driver on a SLES 15 SP6 node for SUSE AI?
output:
As root on a registered SLES 15 SP6 host:
1. Add the NVIDIA CUDA repository for utilities: `zypper ar https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/sles15/x86_64/ cuda-sle15`, then `zypper --gpg-auto-import-keys refresh`.
2. Install the open driver KMP: `zypper install -y --auto-agree-with-licenses nv-prefer-signed-open-driver`. Then record its version: `version=$(rpm -qa --queryformat '%{VERSION}\n' nv-prefer-signed-open-driver | cut -d "_" -f1 | sort -u | tail -n 1)`.
3. Optionally install `nvidia-compute-utils-G06=${version}` and `nvidia-persistenced=${version}`.
4. Reboot, then run `nvidia-smi` to confirm the GPU is detected.
This example uses the G06 driver generation, the most common choice for modern GPUs.

instruction: How do I check that the NVIDIA GPU Operator is working on my RKE2 cluster?
output:
After about a minute:
1. `kubectl get node $NODENAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}' | grep "nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.driver"` should show `pre-installed`.
2. `kubectl get node $NODENAME -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable}'` should list `"nvidia.com/gpu":` with the GPU count.
3. `ls /usr/local/nvidia/toolkit/nvidia-container-runtime` should show the runtime installed by the toolkit daemonset.
4. `grep nvidia /var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml` should show the NVIDIA runtime in the containerd config.
5. Run a test pod that requests `nvidia.com/gpu: 1`, such as the `nvcr.io/nvidia/k8s/cuda-sample:nbody` benchmark.

instruction: How do I let Podman BCI containers on my Fedora laptop use the full SLES repos? I have a SLES subscription.
output:
1. Get `SCCcredentials` from a registered SLES system. You can produce one with `podman run --rm registry.suse.com/suse/sle15:latest bash -c "zypper -n in SUSEConnect; SUSEConnect --regcode REGISTRATION_CODE; cat /etc/zypp/credentials.d/SCCcredentials"`.
2. For interactive containers, mount it: `podman run -v /path/to/SCCcredentials:/etc/zypp/credentials.d/SCCcredentials -it --pull=always registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:latest`.
3. For builds, pass it as a secret, for example with `buildah bud --layers --secret=id=SCCcredentials,src=/path/to/SCCcredentials .`, instead of copying it into the image.
`container-suseconnect` then adds the SLES repositories when Zypper runs.

instruction: Show me a minimal Dockerfile using a SUSE BCI that serves a page with Python.
output:
From the SUSE container guide:
```
FROM registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7
RUN zypper --non-interactive in python3 && \
    echo "Hello Green World!" > index.html
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/python3", "-m", "http.server"]
EXPOSE 8000
```
Build it with `docker build .` or `buildah bud .`. Then run it with `docker run -p 8000:8000 --rm -d IMAGE_ID` and test with `curl localhost:8000`. Use `--non-interactive` with Zypper because you cannot answer prompts during a build.

instruction: What should I do to prepare a SLES 15 SP7 server before upgrading it to SLES 16.0?
output:
1. Install the latest updates with `zypper patch`, and make sure the system is registered with SCC or RMT.
2. Read the release notes for hardware, package or installation-specific issues.
3. Back up configuration, mainly `/etc` and parts of `/var` and `/opt`.
4. Check free disk space, and shut down any KVM guests.
5. Note that root SSH login is disabled by default in SLE 16. To keep it during migration, create `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-permit-root-login.conf` with `PermitRootLogin yes`.
Also check that the OS is on a single partition and that you have SSH key-based login, because only key-based SSH works during the upgrade.

instruction: How do I install SUSE AI Factory from the Rancher Prime UI?
output:
You need Rancher Prime Administrator privileges.
1. In local › Apps › Repositories, click Create, choose OCI Repository, give it a name such as `suse-aif-operator`, and enter `oci://ghcr.io/suse/chart/aif-operator` with no authentication.
2. In Apps › Charts, filter by that repository, click Refresh all repositories, and open the aif-operator tile.
3. Click Install this version, select the `aif-operator` namespace and a name. Optionally customize the Helm options, for example to add registry credentials.
4. Click Install and confirm it appears under Apps › Installed Apps.

instruction: How do I verify the signature of an Application Collection container image?
output:
1. Get your Application Collection credentials (username plus access token, or a service account).
2. Run the Application Collection cosign image against the image and the public key, for example:
`docker run --rm dp.apps.rancher.io/containers/cosign:2 verify dp.apps.rancher.io/containers/etcd:3.5.12 --registry-username USERNAME --registry-password PASSWORD --key https://apps.rancher.io/ap-pubkey.pem`
3. A successful check reports that the cosign claims were validated and the signatures verified against the key.
To verify a single-architecture image, get its digest first with `crane digest --platform linux/amd64 ...` and verify `IMAGE@DIGEST`.

instruction: What are the main steps of a manual SLES 16 installation with Agama on x86_64?
output:
1. Boot the Agama-based ISO and select agama-installer in the GRUB menu.
2. Select SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and accept the license.
3. Set a hostname. It is used for SCC registration, and otherwise the system registers as `agama`.
4. Register with your registration code and optional e-mail.
5. Optionally adjust localization, network and software, such as KVM or Cockpit, and choose the storage device and space policy.
6. Create a non-root user, because root SSH access is disabled by default, and set root authentication.
7. Click Install, wait for it to finish, reboot and log in to verify.

instruction: How do I remove an add-on module from SLES 15 using YaST, including its packages?
output:
1. Start YaST › Software › Add-On Products.
2. Select the module or extension and click Delete, then confirm the warning that its packages will be removed.
3. In the Software Manager, accept removal of all listed packages. If you keep any, at least remove the module's `*-release` package, because kept packages no longer get updates.
4. Finish with Accept and OK.
Never delete the Basesystem Module, and deleting Server Applications is not recommended.

instruction: How do I add another module, like Web and Scripting, to an already registered SLES 15 machine using YaST?
output:
1. Start YaST › Software › System Extensions.
2. Select the modules or extensions you want. Extensions need additional registration codes, and modules they depend on are selected automatically.
3. YaST registers them with the registration server and adds their repositories.
4. The package installer opens with the release packages and defaults preselected. Keep them, add anything else, and finish with Accept.

instruction: How do I check whether a particular SUSE BCI tag is fully supported before I adopt it?
output: Check the `com.suse.supportlevel` label of the exact tag you plan to use. Without pulling, run for example `skopeo inspect docker://registry.suse.com/bci/bci-micro:15.7 | jq '.Labels["com.suse.supportlevel"]'`. `l3` means full SUSE support, while `techpreview` or `unsupported` mean it is not supported for production. The registry.suse.com web UI shows the same information for each image. Values can differ between service packs and between images.

instruction: How do I make Podman on SUSE Linux Micro find images on Docker Hub when I use short names?
output:
By default only the SUSE Registry is configured, and Docker Hub and the openSUSE registry are not. Add them to `/etc/containers/registries.conf`:
`unqualified-search-registries = ["registry.suse.com", "registry.opensuse.org", "docker.io"]`
Then pull with `podman pull SOURCE`. Podman tries each registry in order when you give no registry name. SUSE Linux Micro has no image-building tools, so images always come from a registry.
